TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
ROYAL COMMISSION ON ANTISEMITISM
AND SOCIAL COHESION
THURSDAY, 20 AUGUST 2026
AT 10:00 AM (AEST)
HEARING BLOCK 9, DAY 4
THE HONOURABLE VIRGINIA BELL AC SC,
COMMISSIONER
RICHARD LANCASTER SC, ZELIE HEGER SC, TAMARA PHILLIPS AND
JANE TAYLOR, COUNSEL ASSISTING
PETER MELICAN WITH DR DAVID BLUMENTHAL, THE
COMMONWEALTH OF AUSTRALIA
JOE EDWARDS, THE STATE OF NEW SOUTH WALES
NICHOLAS BENDER SC, VARIOUS JEWISH COMMUNAL BODIES
TRENT GLOVER SC, AUSTRALIAN HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSION
ADAM HOCROTH SC, WITNESS KATE ROSENBERG

<THE HEARING RESUMED AT 10.00 AM
MS HEGER SC: Commissioner, I call Commissioner Sivaraman and Commissioner Kiss
from the Australian Human Rights Commission.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
<GIRIDHARAN SIVARAMAN, AFFIRMED
<KATIE KISS, AFFIRMED
MS HEGER SC: Commissioner Sivaraman, could you please state your name for the
record?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Giridharan Sivaraman.
MS HEGER SC: And you are the Race Discrimination Commissioner?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Correct.
MS HEGER SC: And you have prepared a witness statement dated 14 August 2026?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Correct.
MS HEGER SC: Do you have a copy of that statement there with you?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: I do.
MS HEGER SC: Is it still true and correct to the best of your knowledge and belief?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: It is.
MS HEGER SC: I tender that statement, Commissioner. It's STAT.8999.0001.0641_R.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, the statement will be admitted.
MS HEGER SC: And, Commissioner Kiss, could you please state your name?
COMMISSIONER KISS: Katie Kiss.
MS HEGER SC: And you have prepared a statement dated 19 August 2026?
COMMISSIONER KISS: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: And do you have a copy of that there with you as well?
COMMISSIONER KISS: Yes.

MS HEGER SC: And is that still true and correct to the best of your knowledge and
belief?
COMMISSIONER KISS: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: Commissioner, I tender that statement, which is STAT.8999.0001.0658.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, that statement will also be received.
MS HEGER SC: And, Commissioner Kiss, you are, of course, the Aboriginal and Torres
Strait Islander Social Justice Commissioner?
COMMISSIONER KISS: I am.
MS HEGER SC: And I should note the Human Rights Commission has also provided
a submission to the Royal Commission dated 12 June 2026, and I tender that submission as
well, Commissioner, SUB.5000.0001.4426.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, the submission will be received as an exhibit.
MS HEGER SC: And I'll also tender the Human Rights Commission's report on the
National Anti-Racism Framework, which is DHA.0003.0009.2331.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, the report is admitted.
MS HEGER SC: And in the course of the questions today, I will also be referring to the
Human Rights Commission's Seen & Heard report, that has previously been tendered as
Exhibit 4-015.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: Commissioner Sivaraman, could I start by asking you some questions
about your professional background. So you've held the position of Race Discrimination
Commissioner since March 2024?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Correct.
MS HEGER SC: And prior to your appointment, you worked as a lawyer, predominantly
employment lawyer; is that right?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes, employment and discrimination law.
MS HEGER SC: You have previously been the Chair of Multicultural Australia?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes.

MS HEGER SC: And a member of the Queensland Multicultural Advisory Council.
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: And, Commissioner Kiss, you have described yourself in your
statement as a proud Kaanju and Birri/Widi woman from Queensland?
COMMISSIONER KISS: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: You have held the position of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
Social Justice Commissioner since 2024?
COMMISSIONER KISS: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: And you were formerly the executive director of the Interim Truth and
Treaty Body supporting Queensland's Path to Treaty; is that right?
COMMISSIONER KISS: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: And you also spent eight years previously at the Human Rights
Commission as the Director of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Social Justice team.
COMMISSIONER KISS: That's correct.
MS HEGER SC: Now, Commissioner Sivaraman, could I start by asking you what your
responsibilities are as Race Discrimination Commissioner?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Thank you. My responsibilities are set out in the
Racial Discrimination Act. They're about raising awareness, advocacy and assisting to
eliminate all forms of racial discrimination within Australia, and within that, there's
a broad remit of work that I do including community engagement, engagement with
stakeholders, preparing educational and other materials and advocacy.
MS HEGER SC: And, Commissioner Kiss, could I ask you what your responsibilities
include?
COMMISSIONER KISS: Sure. My role requires me to report on the exercise and
enjoyment of human rights by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, promote
education and awareness on the rights of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, and
to examine legislation and other enactments to make sure that they're consistent with
human rights standards.
MS HEGER SC: Thank you. And could I start by asking you about a topic that you have
both addressed in your statement, which is the meaning of the phrase "social cohesion".
Commissioner Sivaraman, you have identified in your statement that this is an issue that
you've consulted on with communities affected by racism; is that right?

COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: And in light of those discussions, can you describe what those
communities have told you about how they perceive the concept of social cohesion?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes. I think I might start answering it this
way: The question often that comes up in terms of engagement with communities is what
kind of society do we want? And generally, it's - consistently, it's a society where we can
all live with equity, dignity and respect and we all feel a sense of inclusion and belonging,
whether it be in workplaces, public spaces, accessing healthcare, whatever it might be.
You could call that social cohesion. But with the communities that I engage with, their
view and their experience and those principles and those ideas are often not achieved and,
in fact, are counter to government policies, laws and reactions, including in response to the
horrific antisemitic massacre in Bondi.
What they say to me is, often in the name of social cohesion, government policies and
ideas will homogenise entire communities, treating them all the same, dictate to
communities as to what they should do rather than consulting with them and engaging with
them in a meaningful way, pit communities against each other, which is in the sense of
creating a competition for resources or a competition to be heard, which often means that
communities feel isolated, left behind or not seen or heard. And all of these things have
been done in the name of social cohesion, and these things sometimes have the impact of
forcing communities and community members to shed themselves of their language, their
religion, their culture, their dress, the things that make them different in a slow process of
assimilation, which is done, again, in the name of social cohesion, but doesn't enable
a sense of inclusion or belonging, doesn't allow people to live with equity, dignity and
respect.
And in my consultations with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, which
I'm sure Commissioner Kiss will also speak to, there's a fundamental problem in that the
notion of social cohesion doesn't reflect their particular position in our society, their need
for self-determination and sovereignty and their connection to this land. So, in that sense,
that's where the concept of social cohesion has run counter to what it might be aiming to
achieve, and I think it's why many of the communities I engage with view the term with
great wariness and view any kind of policy or plan associated with it with wariness.
But I think that if you - if we want to build a society where we live with equity, dignity and
respect and we feel included and belonging, then you actually have to do the hard work
first of building racial literacy, building the way in which people understand each other and
see diversity as a strength, and building institutions and systems that are transparent,
responsive and accountable to everyone. And that means irrespective of your racial or
religious background, irrespective of gender, of disability, of age, of class, that those
systems and institutions are responsive, inclusive and accountable for you. That is the way
in which - that is the hard work that has to be done first before you can achieve what you
might call social cohesion. And that hard work is ultimately the goal of anti-racism.

MS HEGER SC: I see. I might come back to this point about the connection between
social cohesion and anti-racism but, Commissioner Kiss, could I ask you to comment on
this topic particularly with regard to what your consultations with First Peoples has
revealed with the concept of social cohesion?
COMMISSIONER KISS: Thank you for the question. And on behalf of the two oldest
living cultures on this continent, I thank you for allowing me to present today and to come
to the Royal Commission and talk about how First Peoples feel about social cohesion and
racism. I will talk from the perspective of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Social
Justice Commissioner. In consultations that I have conducted through the Informing the
Agenda Project, which has informed my Social Justice Report 2025, First Peoples don't
necessarily connect with the term "social cohesion". It's not a term that came up in my
consultations. But they did talk extensively about their experience of racism, about their
experience of the lack of unity in this country, about the lack of recognition of us as First
Peoples, both Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.
They talk about the need for recognition and respect, hence the Voice referendum and the
call from First Peoples through the Uluru Statement from the Heart for that constitutional
recognition because for generations, since first contact, 237 years, we have had to fight to
be recognised in what is our own country, our own lands. We have had to fight for equal
participation. We have had to fight for equal consideration in policies, laws and practices
that have had an impact on us, both detrimental and positive. We have had to fight for
everything that has enabled us to effectively participate in the Australian society.
Self-determination is something that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people connect
with. But it's not just self-determination for us; it's being able to participate in the
democracy and have your identity, your cultural background, your status as a citizen of
Australia respected and protected within the laws and policies. So a position that has come
from First Peoples is that while dealing with antisemitism is absolutely important, dealing
with First Peoples' racism is equally important, and the view of First Peoples is that until
you start to address the original racism that was foundational to the building of the
Australian community, you won't be able to address racism against any other community
that has since come and settled in this country.
MS HEGER SC: In light of that feedback that you have had on the concept of social
cohesion, if one understands it in the manner set out in this Commission's Terms of
Reference as a national consensus in support of democracy, freedom and the rule of law,
do you still see that as a useful concept to be deployed from a policy perspective?
COMMISSIONER KISS: I do. Although First Peoples don't see themselves as part of
the social fabric of Australia and they don't see themselves captured within that broader
democratic landscape. We are still on the fringes. We are still on the outer of that, and
every day we are fighting for that inclusion, participation, dignity, respect, equity,
responsive, inclusive and accountable consideration of who we are as the First Peoples.

MS HEGER SC: And, Commissioner Sivaraman, could I ask you to the same question in
light of the feedback that you've received. Do you still see social cohesion as a useful
concept to be pursued?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: In and of itself, it can be, but the problem is it means
so many different things to different people. You could ask 20 people in a room, “what
does social cohesion mean to you?” and you would probably get 20 different answers, and
even the definition used in the Terms of Reference for the Royal Commission about
a national consensus in support of democracy, that's a conclusion, in a sense. It's how do
you get to that point? How do you build a sense of belonging, inclusion, participation,
legitimacy? I'm drawing on terms used by the New Zealand Christchurch attack Royal
Commission.
And so I think its utility is only, again, if you accept that, well, you're not going to this
point by first understanding how inequity operates in our society and how some people are
disadvantaged and how that is done in a systemic way and then trying to improve those
systems and institutions. I think isolated from that, the term, it probably has limited utility.
MS HEGER SC: And so if we strip away the language of social cohesion for a moment
and just focus on the aim of building a national consensus in support of democracy,
freedom and the rule of law, do I understand your evidence correctly that you see those as
legitimate aims to be pursued, but the big question is how do you get there, and one key
part of getting there, in your view, is addressing racism?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes, absolutely. Because you - addressing racism is
about enabling people to participate in a democracy, not just in the very narrow sense of
being able to vote or engage with politics; in a much broader sense of engaging equally in
civic society, engaging across all aspects of public life. So I think the short answer is yes,
and there's a much longer discussion to be had about that, but we should - in identifying
the goal, we should be clear about the obstacles that prevent us from getting there.
MS HEGER SC: Would you like to comment on that as well, Commissioner Kiss?
COMMISSIONER KISS: Just to say in the context of democracy and ensuring a unified
approach values - to the underpinning of the state, it must be without an expectation of
assimilation and integration, and so for First Peoples, that is something that I heard
throughout my consultations, that our participation in the broader Australian community is
requiring us to assimilate, requiring us to integrate and to take on and leave behind who we
are as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander First Peoples.
MS HEGER SC: I then wanted to move to the relationship between social cohesion and
anti-racism, which you have already addressed to some extent in your answers. And,
Commissioner Kiss, you address this at about paragraph 3 and onwards of your statement.
I wanted to ask you - and you've made the point already, I think, that, in your view, social
cohesion is not possible until we address the racism that First Peoples have experienced.
You've also made a point in your statement about how you see trust as an important
concept in all of this, particularly at paragraph 6. Can I ask you what you mean by trust?

Do you mean trust between members of the community or trust between the community
and government or both?
COMMISSIONER KISS: It's both. Australians - let me start again. Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander peoples, First Peoples, have consistently come to the table seeking
the ability to engage with the broader Australian community in genuine good faith. Some
of those conversations are had genuinely back with us, and some of them are not, and the
exposure to racism throughout history has been pervasive and ongoing and consistent. In
terms of trust, when you can't engage safely in public debate, in political debate in broader
community conversations about how we fit within our society, that erodes trust. It erodes
people's sense of belonging. It erodes people's ability to be proud in their own identity and
to participate without question.
And so when you are talking about trust, that comes at an interpersonal level. You know,
when you are out in the shopping centre and you're being followed by security guards you
are not feeling safe in the community in which you exist. When you are tagged along by
police, you are not feeling safe in the community in which you live because those
institutions are meant to protect everybody in the community, not just parts of it. In terms
of the systems and structures, again we have engaged in genuine good faith in order to
build a cohesive community, society, values that also see Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander peoples as part of the community. And time and time again, we have had that
trust dismantled, taken from us, denied because of the way that engagement has come back
to us. So we engage in genuine good faith and we very regularly get denied an equal
response, if I can say that as diplomatically as possible.
MS HEGER SC: And, Commissioner Sivaraman, do you see that concept of trust
between the community and with government as important in addressing all forms of
racism, including antisemitism?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes, absolutely. And I think that's - in a sense, one
of the significant issues is a lack of trust from communities who are affected by racism
because of the use of the term "social cohesion" because of the things that have been done
under that banner, so to speak. Because if your experience of policies or laws or programs
under the term "social cohesion" are ones where you are excluded or you are competing for
resources with other communities or you have to assimilate, as Commissioner Kiss said,
you won't have trust in the institutions you are engaging with. And I think it's also because
that term is used to obscure your experience of racism. I've had someone say to me
in - very senior in government, "Stop talking about racism because you are disrupting the
social cohesion". And I think that sentence encapsulates the difficulty sometimes with that
term, because if it's obscuring, then it's not solving the systemic or structural problem that
you need to fix.
MS HEGER SC: And you've also made the comment in your statement that not only can
social cohesion not be achieved by obscuring racism, but it can't be achieved if you assume
all experiences of racism are the same.
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes. That's correct.

MS HEGER SC: Could you speak to that point?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: I think that's an important point. Every experience
of racism is different and unique. Antisemitism is unique in the way in which it will
impact on people and the people on whom it will impact. The source, though, is often
a systemic issue. So you have to fix the systemic problem to get to the particular impact or
where it manifests in a particular form. But, again, to try and homogenise all experiences
of racism is not something that we say should be done in any of our work or in the
National Anti-Racism Framework. To put it in a simple way, we say that there are
systemic problems that lead to the manifestation of racism. If you don't fix the systemic
problem, the racism will continue to manifest. How it manifests and how it impacts on
people is always going to vary, depending on the community and the person. But if you
keep trying to attack it at that point where it manifests, you are playing Whack-A-Mole
rather than actually trying to do the hard work of the systemic change.
MS HEGER SC: I might come back to that theme when we discuss the National
Anti-Racism Framework, which I'll turn to now. Could I start just by asking you,
Commissioner Sivaraman, to give an overview of the nature and purpose of the
framework, in general terms?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes. So the framework came about as a result of
community agitation to government that there needed to be some sort of National
Framework or strategy to tackle racism, and then preparing it, the Human Rights
Commission engaged in very significant consultation with community members,
government departments, business, decision-makers and experts. Importantly that is not
just people affected by racism. It's leaders, decision-makers, who themselves might not be
affected by racism but have the capacity to bring about change.
MS HEGER SC: Just pausing there, did that consultation with leaders include within
government and outside of government, in business and the like?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes. Correct.
MS HEGER SC: I see. Please continue.
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: And what consistently came through in all of our
consultations was - and this was supported by research - is that government responses to
racism have been ad hoc and piecemeal and, in fact, Yamagigu, which was then PwC
Indigenous, prepared a report for us which showed exactly that. Some parts of government
don't even want to use the word "racism". That ad hoc and piecemeal approach is one that
communities highlighted to us as a severe impediment to actually genuinely tackling
racism, and it also came through in our individual consultations. So it was through that
research and those consultations that we created the National Anti-Racism Framework, and
we knew it was broad in scope and bold in its ambition, but it had to be because we are
trying to tackle a fundamental problem within society.

But knowing that, that is why the primary recommendation in that framework was to set up
a taskforce with government, community and industry representatives to identify which
recommendations to implement as a matter of priority and to work through how to
implement them. And, critically, it also contained a provision for monitoring,
accountability and evaluation, because we know that there's actually very little evaluation
of how successful anti-racism work is, to the extent that it's done. And so we think that if
you are going to do it, you are going to have to measure the success of it, and that's part of
the framework too.
MS HEGER SC: And that framework was published in November 2024? Is that right?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Correct.
MS HEGER SC: And included 63 recommendations for the reform of various systems
and structures, including across seven key areas of the legal system, health, education,
workplaces, media and the arts, data collection; is that right?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes, those were the areas that came through in our
consultations as the most critical to move on.
MS HEGER SC: Has the government responded to those recommendations at this point
in time?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: The only response that I have received is that they're
considering the framework. As of today, that's all I've got.
MS HEGER SC: And, Commissioner Kiss, could I ask, do you consider a framework of
this kind to be an important thing and why you hold that view?
COMMISSIONER KISS: Absolutely. The National Anti-Racism Framework is
a milestone in terms of addressing racism in Australia. It recognises that you can't confine
racism to individual experiences of racism. It looks at the structural and systemic response
required to address it. For First Peoples, it provides a practical roadmap through the
recommendation on National Taskforce for First Nations to Address Racism. It also is
consistent with the national government's Closing the Gap policy approach and the
National Agreement to Closing the Gap which requires, under priority reform 3, that we
eliminate racism in all government agencies and structures and policies.
It understands and it reflects the fact that you can't separate racism from the colonial
foundations of Australia, the dispossession of First Peoples, the minimising of the history
of this country and then blaming First Peoples for the outcomes of that. So the framework
is absolutely critical to us advancing anti-racism work in the country for all people who are
subjected to racism, not just First Peoples, but it centres First Peoples, as I say, at the
beginning of the conversation, dealing with the racism that is experienced by First Peoples
as the centre of the conversation in Australia, and the fact that other racism that occurs
happens in that context.

MS HEGER SC: And, Commissioner Sivaraman, you have touched on this in answer to
an earlier question but you've noted in your statement at paragraph 26 that changing
behaviours can only occur by changing systems and institutions. Could I ask you to
elaborate on that point?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes. It's probably easiest to explain that through
examples. So you have identified the areas in which we focus, but let's just take
workplaces as a particular example. So you could counsel the perpetrator of an antisemitic
slur in a workplace. That isn't going to stop all antisemitic slurs within that workplace.
What you actually have to do is a systemic review and identify, for example, is the
workplace culturally safe? Is there - are there effective anti-racism policies? Is there a
complaints mechanism that ensures there isn't victimisation? If you don't bring about those
kinds of systemic changes, you will never eradicate all of the racist behaviour.
And so that is why we say if you genuinely want to stop racism and do it in a way that
addresses all racism, you do it through systemic change, and you start with that. That's the
platform for doing it. There are similar examples we could give in health and education.
I will give one more because I think it's a good one. Social media, you could remove
a user of social media who has put an antisemitic slur online. Everyone in this room
knows there is no way that is going to stop all antisemitism that is online. So unless you
bring about systemic change in terms of countering mis- and disinformation and breaking
the nexus between profit and racism for social media platforms, you will never stop racism
online. Again, another example of why we believe that systems change is the only way to
actually bring about meaningful change.
MS HEGER SC: And on that point, one aspect of the framework is addressing the online
environment to some extent, for example, I think, it favours the imposition of an additional
duty of care.
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Correct.
MS HEGER SC: Yes, which we have heard evidence about in other contexts in the Royal
Commission. Could I ask you this: You gave evidence earlier about specific forms of
racism and recognised that each is unique. The framework, of course, is expressed in
terms of racism generally, as opposed to particular kinds of racism. And the Commission
has received some public submissions that express the perspective that, for that reason, the
framework could be seen to diminish or fail to address what are unique characteristics of
different types of racism, including antisemitism. What's your response to that sort of
concern?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: So every day I engage with communities that are
impacted by racism, and for them, it can be a terrible issue that requires an
urgent response. And many of those communities don't think that they're reflected or seen
or heard or listened to at all by government or by others. If we don't come up with
a solution, start with a platform that addresses all form of racism - all forms of racism,
sorry - we continue to leave those communities behind. That in itself is a significant
problem because it leads to a sense of isolation and of being alienated by those

communities and people within them. That is not going to contribute to a society where
people feel included or belong or safe.
The National Anti-Racism Framework as a foundation for work ensures, firstly, that all
communities get consulted with in terms of the design of solutions, and that's a really
significant point in anti-racism work, rather than just some communities. And as I've said
earlier, it stops communities from being pitted against each other. And then it allows
a systems change. So, for example, one of the proposals in the National Anti-Racism
Framework is a positive duty to eliminate racial discrimination in workplaces and then,
more broadly, within goods and services. So the system change there is that you bring
about a positive duty to eliminate racism.
Let's take workplaces as an example. In them doing that work, you would have to go
through a number of measures, including assessing how your organisation is travelling,
because then you can create targeted programs to deal with the racism that is manifesting
in your organisation. You could survey your workers. And when you then create those
tailored programs, you absolutely can address specific forms of racism; in fact, you have
to. That's the natural thing that would come after having done the work of actually
assessing what it is the organisation requires. So of course you could target antisemitism
and you should, and you could target other forms of racism as well. I think that's the thing
that people forget in the sense it's not just about generic training. That in itself is not
a solution. An actual whole-of-organisation solution would be to evaluate where your
organisation is at, using something like the Workplace Cultural Diversity Tool that the
Human Rights Commission offers, survey your workforce, work out where you need to
bring about change, implement that change in a tailored way that caters to the communities
you are trying to help, and then monitor and evaluate how successful that has been.
MS HEGER SC: And so this ties into your point at paragraph 24 of your statement, does
it, where you say the framework recommendations have capacity to tailor solutions to suit
the needs of affected communities, including those experiencing antisemitism?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes, absolutely. And, on that account - I don't want
to take up too much time. I can give you one more example, I think, that might help
illustrate the point.
MS HEGER SC: Certainly.
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: And that's another of our recommendations is
a national survey on racism and, of course - so the starting point is you are doing a national
survey, so you get to hear from everyone. And of course you would then have to measure
particular types of racism within that survey including antisemitism, and other forms of
racism as well. So it is a solution to tackle all forms of racism that clearly can be
tailored - it would have to be tailored - to particular experiences. A bit like we did with
our survey in the university sector, where we got 76,000 responses, including a significant
response from Jewish students and staff, where we could identify specific forms of racism
and what was required, but we started with an approach where we tried to hear from
everyone.

MS HEGER SC: And so, just so I understand your evidence, you're not excluding the
utility of, in a workplace, having targeted antisemitism training, for example?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: No, I'm not excluding targeting - targeted
campaigns for antisemitism, no.
MS HEGER SC: I see. And, Commissioner Kiss, I take it your view is that a broad
framework of this kind is capable of achieving something in terms of addressing the
unique nature of racism experienced by First Peoples?
COMMISSIONER KISS: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: Is that your view?
COMMISSIONER KISS: Yes. I think there needs to be - you know, Commissioner
Sivaraman has talked about workplace initiatives to help mitigate the instances of racism in
workplaces. I think those sorts of things help to combat racism against all people in
workplaces, but also things like cultural safety frameworks, which the Commission has
been working through, to make sure that our organisation is culturally safe. Those sorts of
things. Reconciliation Action Plans, accountability measures within workplaces, so zero
tolerance of racism within workplaces, all those things contribute to make sure that
everyone is safe in the workplace but also that First Peoples are captured within that.
MS HEGER SC: Could I then come to ask you about some of the recommendations that
are made as part of that framework. So, Commissioner Sivaraman, you have already
explained how you see one important first step as being to set up a taskforce to decide
where the prior areas should lie. Commissioner Kiss, could I then ask you about the
concept of a taskforce. You've identified in your statement at about paragraph 27 that you
would see utility in also establishing a First Nations Anti-Racism Taskforce to develop and
implement a dedicated First Nations Anti-Racism Framework Implementation Plan as
well. Could you explain why you see that would be a useful addition, on top of the sort of
taskforce that Commissioner Sivaraman has identified?
COMMISSIONER KISS: Sure. As Commissioner Sivaraman has talked to, the
experience of racism for different community groups is different, and the racism
experienced by First Peoples is unique in the fact that its origins lie in the dispossession,
the discrimination experienced by First Peoples, policies and practices that only impact
First Peoples in Australia, so things like the Protection Acts that resulted in the removal of
children from their families and the Bringing Them Home report recommendations. So the
National Anti-Racism Taskforce for First Peoples enables and creates spaces for First
Peoples to sit at those tables and have their unique issues addressed.
It also helps First Peoples to contribute to the conversation on how we address racism more
broadly, because First Peoples also feel a responsibility for those who now live on our
lands and territories. We feel that responsibility very deeply, and we want to make sure
that we are also making contributions to ensuring that racism is not more broader than our

communities but also that we are addressing the racism that we experience on a day-to-day
basis. There's a tendency to invisiblise First Peoples' experience of racism. And so when
things like multiculturalism debates are being heard, First Nations racism sits over here in
the corner and nobody is talking about that. We forget to deal with the broadness of it. So
this enables First Peoples to have a space at the table in their own right to deal with the
origins of racism for Australia, as well as contributing to an anti-racism approach that
makes sure that everyone else feels safe as well.
MS HEGER SC: Then, Commissioner Sivaraman, could I come back to the idea of
imposing a positive duty. And that would be a positive duty to eliminate racial
discrimination in the workplace; is that what you envisage?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: And can you explain a little more what the nature of that proposed duty
would look like?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes. So as it's - currently, if you are the target of
racism in the workplace, you have to have suffered harm, really, to seek recourse, and the
Racial Discrimination Act turned 50 last year and it's time for that to change. It's time to
put the onus and the emphasis on the entities with the capacity and the resources to bring
about the change. It's a far more effective way to eliminate racial discrimination. So it
would - and we have seen something similar already happen in the changes to the Sex
Discrimination Act, which created a positive duty to eliminate sexual harassment. So it
would require organisations, workplaces, to - well, I think best practice would be to
actually survey your employees, to review your policies and procedures, like using the tool
that I described earlier, ascertain the areas in which you need improvement, and then
probably create a committee that can help do that, co-design solutions, but without putting
all of the effort on to that group, particularly if it's a group with people that are affected by
racism, and then monitor and evaluate your changes over time.
MS HEGER SC: And so what you have just stepped through, those are all measures that
might be taken in order to fulfil the positive duty, that is, surveying, establishing some kind
of action plan and then implementing it; is that right?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Correct, that's right.
MS HEGER SC: And so what are some examples of - and I appreciate this will depend
upon the particular workplace - the sorts of actions that might be implemented in order to
further fulfil that positive duty? It might be training on particular forms of racism or
racism generally in a particular workplace, for example?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes. So I think a starting point would be, before
you get to the training, it's actually creating a specific anti-racism policy or strategy within
your workplace, rather than having it subsumed within general equity, diversity and
inclusion policies, as is often the case. And then once you have established that - and
doing that should be done in a consultative and careful way - you could then provide

training to staff and employees, anti-racism training. Hopefully training is informed by the
work you had done previously so it can be targeted and more effective.
MS HEGER SC: And can I ask, have you consulted with businesses and government
workplaces as well about the practicability of implementing something like this and what
sort of feedback have you received?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes, I have. And it's actually been pretty good
engagement. I'm not - I'm yet to have an employer that says to me, "I don't want to have to
eliminate racial discrimination in the workplace." But I think, more importantly,
employers I have engaged with and employer representative groups I have engaged with
have said, "Look, we can see an advantage in this, because at the moment, particularly
when we operate between different jurisdictions our responsibilities will change because
some jurisdictions, some state and territory jurisdictions have a positive duty to eliminate
racial discrimination and other forms of discrimination; others don't."
Whereas if you have an overarching national obligation to do it, informed by guidelines on
how to do it - and the Victorian Human Rights and Equal Opportunities Commission
Guidelines to Eliminating Racial Discrimination is an excellent one that I think the
Commission should have regard to - then it becomes an easier thing to do, because you are
complying with the national standard and it doesn't matter which jurisdiction you are
moving between; you can do it. And the other reason I think that it's had support is that,
from an employer - the employers and employer representative bodies I've engaged with
can see great value in it. They want workforces that feel included, that belong, that are
productive, that are happy. If eliminating racial discrimination is a way of enabling that,
that's a good thing. It's a good thing for the workplace; it's a good thing for the employer.
So, in that sense, I've generally had quite positive engagement on the issue.
COMMISSIONER: Have you engaged with medium and smaller size enterprises?
I mean, it's one thing to imagine that BHP could probably implement a scheme of the kind
you describe, albeit there would be economic consequences to it doing so, but for
a relatively small enterprise, the imposition of yet another duty might be something that is
really quite difficult for them to achieve. I just don't know how wide your consultation has
been, and that's what I'm asking.
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes, that's a - I understand that, Commissioner, and
I think that's why in the framework, when we talk about anti-racism strategies within
workplaces, we specifically talk about medium to large-size workplaces, because we
recognise that the imposition on small workplaces would be far more onerous. And
certainly I don't discount the difficulty of a regulatory burden. And some employer
representatives talk about that. So I'm not - I'm completely alive to that, and they're alive
to that. That's why I put it in the sense of if there can be an advantage of actually making
life easier, it could be a good thing.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.

MS HEGER SC: You have also identified, Commissioner Sivaraman, in your statement,
some of what you consider to be the priority areas in terms of the recommendations that
have been made. Can I ask you about those. So the first point relates to a National
Anti-Racism Data Plan. What does that involve and why do you consider that to be an
important thing?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: So if we want to know whether our anti-racism
measures are effective, we need to have data on the incidences of racism. As it - we don't
have good data on that. We don't even have a question in the census on ethnicity. We've
just got proxy questions about people's ancestry. We don't have a national mechanism for
collecting data on incidences of racism. So what is reported, for example, or what is
complained about is just a microcosm of what actually occurs, and the obligation often
falls on community groups - who do a good job and the best they can, like, for example,
the Executive Council of Australian Jewry in terms of antisemitism; Islamophobia Register
for Islamophobia; or Call it Out Register for First Peoples racism. But that is a huge
obligation on small organisations without resources, and they will readily tell you that
what is reported to them is only ever going to be a fraction of what is actually happening in
the communities they represent.
So that's why we say there needs to be a National Anti-Racism Data Plan, because we also
have to remember that data on race and racial identity, the history of collection of that data
in this country has not always been for the benefit of those communities. It's often been to
surveil them, to remove them from their families. It's been to their detriment. So we have
to actually think about why are we collecting this data, to what purpose, and ensure that we
do it in an anti-racism way. That's why we say there should be an Anti-Racism Data Plan.
MS HEGER SC: And, Commissioner Kiss, do you see that as important as well,
collecting more data on racism against First Peoples?
COMMISSIONER KISS: Yes. As Commissioner Sivaraman said, data collection in this
country has often been used to our detriment. In terms of understanding the impact of
racism, particularly through those Closing the Gap targets, every one of those targets is
a breach of human rights. In order to measure both progress and lack of progress in the
context of progression towards achieving those targets, we need to understand the extent to
which racism is actually having an impact. And so, as Commissioner Sivaraman has said,
the lack of reporting doesn't give us a full perspective on the reasons or the underpinnings
why we are not seeing progress in key areas to overcome the disadvantage faced by First
Peoples. And measuring racism, we've seen - particularly in the First Nations context,
because we do some initiatives where we are trying to measure the impact of that. So we
have the Call It Out Register. We have the Reconciliation Australia Racism Barometer.
So we are collecting some of that data, but it's not yet being used in ways that can help to
understand how laws, policies and practice continue to cause disadvantage or contribute to
disadvantage for First Peoples and how we can actually use the data to inform how we
improve those outcomes.
MS HEGER SC: And, Commissioner Sivaraman, you are familiar with the working done
on the National Hate Crimes Database, are you, to some extent?

COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: In a general sense, yes. I haven't been party to it.
MS HEGER SC: Do you see that as a useful exercise and what, if anything, additional to
that are you envisaging in terms of data collection.
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: I think it's a useful exercise in terms of nationalising
and having an overarching database about hate crimes, and that's important and what we
learn from it will be important. But, again, it will encounter the same fundamental
problem that it's only going to reflect what is actually being reported, prosecuted and
reported and that is - it's going to be a fraction of what actually happens. The only real
way to get a full understanding of how racism is impacting communities like the Jewish
community and other communities in Australia is through some sort of national survey or
prevalence study, again, like we did in the university sector. And it requires courage,
because nobody is going to be happy when they see the results.
MS HEGER SC: So there seem to be a number of different strands you envisage in terms
of the data collection. One you have mentioned is national surveys, and you've also
mentioned in the framework, I think, this idea that employers should also have an
obligation to report incidents of racism as well? Is that an important part of it, in your
view?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes, absolutely, because if you want genuine
systemic and cultural change within employers, I think that having the obligation to report
on incidences of racism is a very strong tool to do that, and we can see that in the sense of
we have got a Workplace Gender Equality Authority which requires organisations - and, to
your earlier point, Commissioner, it's not all organisations; it's larger ones - to report on
gender equity within the workplace. And it is that requirement to be - I don't want to use
the expression "named and shamed"; let's say being in the public eye in terms of what you
have done, that is going to be the probably biggest impetus for change. And we've seen
that. It has been an impetus for change. So that's the same thing I think that we need in
terms of eliminating racial discrimination.
MS HEGER SC: And in your statement, you have included a table that outlines the
commonalities between the National Anti-Racism Framework, the key actions proposed by
the Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism, as well as the Special Envoy to Combat
Islamophobia, and this focus on data collection seems to be a common element between all
three action plans; is that right?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes, absolutely it is.
MS HEGER SC: Could I then ask you about another priority area you've identified, and
that is mandatory workplace anti-racism training in government workplaces, which also is
reflected in both Special Envoys' plans; correct?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Correct.

MS HEGER SC: To date, the Royal Commission has received some evidence about the
steps being taken to implement antisemitism training in the Australian Public Service, for
example. Are you generally aware of the work being done in that space?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: In a very general sense, very general.
MS HEGER SC: In a general sense. And do you see that model as a useful one? And do
you envisage a model of that kind being deployed but that takes in other forms of racism as
well as part of implementing this recommendation?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: I'm not familiar enough with the model of how the
training will be delivered to comment on how useful it is. I think that - so I couldn't say.
I couldn't comment to that degree.
MS HEGER SC: I see. But, again, your position doesn't exclude training specific to
particular forms of racism in a workplace, but do you see it as essential to also have
general anti-racism training sitting alongside those sorts of specific programs?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes, I think so. I mean, they're not in opposition to
each other. They work closely together, because I think if you are going to train - if you
are going to build in a training program that targets specific forms of racism, which is
entirely appropriate and particularly if you have got a problem with specific forms of
racism, your starting point needs to actually build a sense of racial literacy and an
understanding of what you're trying to achieve and why it's important.
If you just force people to go through training without doing that hard work initially as to
why and what benefits there are in doing so, I don't think it will be overly effective. So I
think the two complement each other really well. And the other things is in terms of an
impost on organisations, in terms of an impost on government, if you are going to do this
and you want to do this in the most effective way possible, then you should be trying to
tackle all forms of racism. Otherwise you will tackle one now and you will tackle another
later and it will become grossly inefficient. So we think that, within government
workplaces, the most efficient productive way to do it is to start by talking about racism in
all forms and then, of course, you can then tailor it to specific communities.
MS HEGER SC: And you have also identified as a priority area mandatory professional
development for primary and secondary school staff on racism and building capability to
discuss it, and this also is reflected in both the Special Envoys’ plans as well. And we've
likewise heard some evidence in the Commission about the pilot program in Victoria and
New South Wales Departments of Education for antisemitism training. Do you have any
familiarity with the nature of that pilot program?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: No, I don't, I'm sorry.
MS HEGER SC: Not in detail, no. But what sort of mandatory professional development
are you envisaging in schools?

COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes. So I think it's important to acknowledge that
it's difficult for teachers, and if you counsel one teacher for failing to act on a racist
incident, you are not going to enable all teachers within an educational institution to act on
racist incidents. If, on the other hand, you have a program that builds skills, tools and
capabilities for teachers to be able to identify and work through what can be very
challenging issues, you've got a much better chance of dealing with the racism there. And
that actually has to be done carefully. So we at the Commission have been writing our
own pilot program in primary schools, and it's been carefully done in that we have engaged
with principals, parents, teachers, the union, community members and elders, to build
a place-based program specific to a number of primary schools.
And I think that that will involve - I don't think; I know that that will involve the training
of teachers and assisting them to build the skills, tools and capability to actually both
themselves understand how to discuss and deal with racism, and how to teach their
students about it as well. So that kind of careful place-based model is one we want to
expand, and we have got an Education Reference Group of teachers and others in the
education field with whom we're talking about, well, how can we best expand
this - because the pilot has been successful - how do we best expand this now more
broadly, a place-based idea or program to a more broader - broadly in the community.
MS HEGER SC: You have also identified as a priority area nationally consistent
anti-racism resources and educational materials for staff and students in curricula that
focus on recognising and rejecting racism, including contemporary forms of racism. Could
at that point, I jump to you, Commissioner Kiss. You have addressed in your statement
how important you consider education and civics education. Could I ask you to speak to
that topic?
COMMISSIONER KISS: Sure. Before I go to that topic, if I can just go back to the data
question?
MS HEGER SC: Certainly.
COMMISSIONER KISS: Under the Closing the Gap agreement, priority reform 4
requires data sovereignty and making sure that First Peoples have control over the
information that is collected on them. As we made the point earlier that a lot of that data
collected has been used to the detriment of First Peoples. So data sovereignty is important,
not just for First Peoples but on all peoples who data is collected for, that they have control
over how the information is being used and to what benefit or detriment the data can be
applied. So I think that's an important point, just to raise there as well, around priority
reform 4 under the Closing the Gap agreement requires that level of data sovereignty in
order to make sure that racism is addressed in the intent in which it is actually intended for.
In terms of education, truth-telling, as we've seen through the many inquiries, the many
reports, the many recommendations that have been issued, but most recently the Yoorrook
Justice Commission, shows how building understanding of the historical circumstances of
First Peoples in Australia contributes to more social cohesion, more understanding on why
First Peoples are in the situation that they're in, why policies, practices and laws have been

established the way they have and the impacts that they've had on the lives of Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
If I can draw on an example, my daughter came home from school one day and said to me,
"Mum, my teacher told me today that Torres Strait Islander people are the same as
Aboriginal people." So even to the point of teachers not having the understanding that
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are two distinct cultural groups creates
tension, creates concern, creates racism against First Peoples in that the teachers can't even
express correct information to students to enable them to understand the difference
between Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, the First Peoples of this country, but
also the historical influence and impact that has been had as a result of policies, laws and
practice.
As we have seen through and from the Yoorrook Commission, governments' participation
in that is critical. Most Australians don't have a reasonable understanding of the impact of
those histories, laws and policies on First Peoples. And so the racism that we are exposed
to comes from that lack of understanding, both from interpersonal perspective but also
from government agencies and how they draft policies, practices, how values are
established in our country and how education institutions actually teach Australians about
how they engage with different population groups in the country, including Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander peoples.
Civics education, we know, is something that needs to be worked on in this country.
People don't understand how democracy works. Just yesterday, I spent the day at
parliament with a group of Torres Strait Islander people, young people included, and they
asked me about what's the difference between the two houses of parliament and how they
operate effectively. So even our own young people who have come through school have
not been taught about how parliamentary systems and the system of democracy and the
rule of law operate, or how it applies to them.
Things like the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, most Australians have no
knowledge that Australia has actually endorsed the declaration, and governments are silent
on its implementation at the moment. And so until Australians have access to information
and access to education that enables them to engage in understanding, knowledge,
information that helps them to understand the situation and circumstances of First Peoples,
the origins of racism against our people, the impact of that on our people - and we talked
earlier about the impact of racism. We know, in our communities, racism is killing our
people.
You only have to go to the target on suicide, which is going backwards, under the Closing
the Gap agreement; a lot of the impact of suicide on our people is the result of the racism
that they are exposed to. So unless we are addressing that from the education system very
early on, we are not going to change the values, we are not going to change the
understanding, we are not going to change the engagement.
I also want to just reflect on my own grandchildren's experience when they go to daycare,
childcare. When they are coming home and they're painting pictures of the Aboriginal and

Torres Strait Islander flag and the pride they feel that their other little Australian
colleagues in their classrooms feel pride in painting those pictures, when they come home
and they've been given boomerangs to paint, at the earliest of the earliest ages, we need to
be teaching young Australians about respect, about inclusion, about pride in the cultures
that make up what is now modern-day Australia. And so, yes, I just reflect on the fact that
even our little people see the pride in that and at what stage does it become something
that's not something to be proud of anymore?
MS HEGER SC: Commissioner Sivaraman, in terms of that recommendation about
resources and the review of the curriculum, are you generally aware of the work that was
done by the Antisemitism Education Taskforce in collaboration with the Curriculum
Review Authority about reviewing the curriculum in terms of antisemitism and how that
does now seem to have been expanded, especially following the Special Envoy for
Islamophobia's recommendations, into a broader review in terms of looking at
incorporating anti-racism and different forms of racism? In terms of that workstream, do
you see that as a useful response to the recommendations that the framework makes or do
you envisage something additional and different to that workstream?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: I think it is a useful response. And my
understanding is it's been expanded to antisemitism and other forms of hate. And I have
had a limited degree of participation in the work that has been led by Mr Gonski. And I
think it's good that it's broadened because curriculum reform is an enormous exercise, and
it's very hard to do. But its impact is equally enormous. So if you are going to do it, don't
do it in a piecemeal way. Try and actually do it in a way that is significant. If you are
going to do it, then do it in a way that deals with all forms of racism in that, when you get
that chance. It's - I guess we will have to see how it unfolds, and I'm - I've just been
consulted with, so I don't know the intimate details of it. But I think in that sense, if the
aim is to incorporate and include all forms of racism, that is absolutely what it should do,
and if it's not doing that, then it should.
COMMISSIONER KISS: Ms Heger, can I just add to that as well. Probably about 10
years ago, the Human Rights Commission did a fair bit of work with the ACARA, the
curriculum development organisation, to embed Indigenous knowledges and Indigenous
perspectives in all aspects of the education curriculum. It didn't get very far. I think the
work was developed, but it didn't get picked up and it hasn't been embedded across the
system. So there's a lot of work that has already been done in that space as well; we just
need to activate it.
MS HEGER SC: And does that tie back to a point made in your statement about
accountability, this gap between, to your observation, commitments and implementation?
COMMISSIONER KISS: Yes.
MS HEGER SC: And do you see the National Anti-Racism Framework as a measure of
accountability?

COMMISSIONER KISS: I think it's one measure of accountability. We talk to the fact
from, a First Nations' perspective, that you need a Human Rights Act in order to make sure
that Australia is compliant with its human rights responsibilities and obligations, that it's
ratified and voluntarily taken up. We talk to the need for the implementation of the
Anti-Racism Framework to create a structure and amend systems that cause damage and
harm from a racism perspective. So we talk about that, and we also talk about the need for
that full implementation on the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples in order to
make sure that, when we are dealing with First Peoples, their rights are being fully
respected. Their rights are - the right to non-discrimination is activated and the guidepost
is the National Anti-Racism Framework and the declaration in tandem.
We talk about they're not being - you can't create reconciliation if we're not having
respectful relationships. And so the accountability measures must be in place. We know
that with the National Agreement on Closing the Gap, there's a requirement for
accountability in there. That accountability measure hasn't been put into place. And so
things like PR3, which is the elimination of racism in our government agencies, hasn't had
any accountability mechanism placed around that to ensure that it's being met.
So while we are trying to deal with racism in a broader sense, there's government
commitments to eradicate racism against First Peoples that are being ignored, that aren't
being activated appropriately within government. And so that accountability then
permeates everything. You know, we are seeing in jurisdictions where policies, laws and
practices that have a significant disproportionate impact on Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander people, including, for example, the adult crime, adult time legislation in
Queensland, where we have made commitments under the Closing the Gap agreement to
reduce the number of children in detention, yet we put laws and policies in place that
actually increase the number of children in detention. And the disproportionate impact of
that is on First Peoples.
During my Informing the Agenda consultations, I visited one of the prisons up in Darwin.
90 per cent Aboriginal in those prisons. So the discriminatory impact on our people is
significant. The other thing around accountability is that we have worked very hard
through things like the 1967 referendum to change the laws and structures that impact on
our people. We worked to amend the constitution to make sure that the Commonwealth
could make laws on behalf of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. We hoped that
that would be in the benefit of our people. But every time the Racial Discrimination Act
has been overridden or suspended has been to the detriment of Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander people: the Hindmarsh Island case, the Native Title Amendment Bill, and the
Northern Territory emergency response. And so that's an indication of what is possible for
other communities who also experience racism where protections are not in place
sufficiently.
MS HEGER SC: Thank you. Commissioner, that concludes my questions on the
Anti-Racism Framework and I now propose to move to some topics that are dealt with in
Commissioner Sivaraman's statement but not in Commissioner Kiss's statement. And so at
that point, I was proposing for Commissioner Kiss to be excused, subject to any further
questions you might have, Commissioner.

COMMISSIONER: Yes. Just one thing, Ms Heger, before we leave the framework that
I might raise with both the Commissioners. I appreciate that there has been a long time
since the publication of the framework and the government's response and that the
government has advised the Commission that the matter is still under consideration. And
I just want to raise with both of you that one can, to a degree at least, understand that long
period of consideration by government, given the breadth of it.
Out of the many recommendations, one is the matter that Commissioner Kiss just referred
to: The enactment of a Human Rights Act, and that has been a highly controversial matter
for many years. There are many proponents in Australia of the idea of a Human Rights
Act, but equally many people of goodwill who say tread warily before that, because it
transfers a degree of power to the courts to determine how human rights rub up against one
another and where one strikes the balance and, to that extent, might politicise the courts.
I'm not expressing a view one way or the other, but what I'm wanting to raise with both of
you is that, in some ways, the sheer breadth of the ambition of the Anti-Racism Framework
might be an impediment to the achievement of some of the priorities.
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Could I respond, Commissioner?
COMMISSIONER: Yes, by all means. I'm inviting it.
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Can I respond in this way. I want to actually
respond by bringing it back to why we're here. We're here because of something horrific
that happened in December last year. We don't know - horrific that happened to Jewish
men, women and children in December last year. We don't know if any one thing could
have stopped that from happening. We know - or, of course, it's alleged that the people
involved, the two people involved, they would have had jobs. One of them went to school
here. There were two touchpoints in the journey of hate that led to its terrible conclusion.
Nobody, I don't think, gets up deciding they're going to do something so hateful or terrible.
There is a journey to get there. And in that journey, there were two points at which
perhaps they could have been diverted from that ultimate destination of hate: workplaces
and education.
So our framework always envisaged that the whole thing wouldn't get implemented at once
and that it was difficult. That is why the primary recommendation was set up a taskforce
identify what to move with as a matter of priority - don't have to do it all. Just what to
move with as a matter of priority. And education and workplaces were absolutely areas we
thought should be moved with as a matter of priority. So I hope that explains to you why it
doesn't have to be the whole thing. It was about identifying what to start with.
COMMISSIONER: It explains it very well. Thank you. Commissioner, Kiss, anything
to add?
COMMISSIONER KISS: Commissioner, just a comment from me in that while
I appreciate the courts' role and the involvement that you've identified, First Peoples,

without the protection of human rights, without the protection of anti-racism strategies and
those sorts of things to combat the harm that's caused as a result of both of those things,
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people have only had the courts to rely on to fight for
our rights. So we have had a Human Rights Commission in place. We have complaints
processes in place. But things like the overturning of terra nullius had to go through the
High Court in order to have that acknowledged. You know, we have had to fight for our
land on justice and dispossession through the courts. We have got people taking police
forces to court now because of the racism they have been exposed to.
COMMISSIONER: I'm not suggesting that we do away with courts, Commissioner Kiss.
COMMISSIONER KISS: No, no, not at all, and I would hope that you wouldn't,
because we have had to rely on them in order to affirm our rights, in the absence of the
protections, yes. Thank you, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: I understand.
