framework are specifically targeted to just medium and large employers and does that
include the positive duty that we discussed earlier?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: So, yes, it was actually, I think, a question from the
Commissioner and, yes, so there's two parts to this. The first is, yes, the recommendations
about developing workplace anti-racism strategies; internal cultural safety frameworks;
strategies for monitoring, hiring and progression of people affected by racism, all of those,
we have explicitly said, are only for medium and large employers because we understand,
as to your point, Commissioner, the obligation could be too onerous for smaller businesses.
And on the second point of a positive duty, we haven't - the framework itself doesn't
specify to whom it would apply, but if you were to take the duty as it has been legislated in
the Sex Discrimination Act as an example, it explicitly, within the framing of the law,

differentiates between what would be required by a small, medium or large business in that
it would only be what was reasonable and proportionate to the size of the business. So,
again, to your point, Commissioner, that's what we would envisage in terms of a positive
duty. So it would accommodate exactly the concern that the Commissioner raised earlier.
MS HEGER SC: I see. Thank you. Could you then move to ask you about the Seen &
Heard Report, which was published earlier this year. So is it right that the Department of
Home Affairs funded the Human Rights Commission to survey the experience of racism
across the Jewish, Muslim, Arab and Palestinian communities from 7 October onwards?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes, it wasn't a survey. This was a quantitative
study. So we were funded by the Department of Home Affairs, and we conducted what
was effectively a qualitative study, because it was 27 community engagements all across
Australia, with Jewish, Palestinian, Muslim and Arab community members to better
understand how they had been impacted by an increase in racism since October 7, 2023.
MS HEGER SC: And how did you go about identifying the individuals or groups who
you engaged with for the purposes of obtaining that qualitative data?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes. So we did it predominantly through
community organisations. So, for example, the Queensland Jewish Board of Deputies
arranged a consultation for us with Jewish community members, which I attended in the
Holocaust Museum in Brisbane. The Australian Palestinian Advocacy Network organised
a consultation with Palestinian community members, and that we found to be the most
effective way to - and probably the safest and best way to get community members
together. Different organisations in different places, but, in a general sense, that's how it
worked.
MS HEGER SC: I see. And what was the overall objective of undertaking that
engagement?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: The objective was first to satisfy the requirement of
the contract entered into with the Department of Home Affairs. The requirement of that
contract was to come up with a campaign to deal with the increased racism since October
7, 2023. Initially, the requirement was only to engage with Muslim, Arab and Palestinian
communities, but we said that it has to be broader than that and it has to engage with the
Jewish community as well, because we don't want to be put in the position of - as I have
repeatedly said earlier - having communities pit against each other.
The second thing is we said that you can't come up with a campaign without first having
significant consultation with those communities as to how they have been affected by
antisemitism, anti-Palestinian racism, Islamophobia, and it was using what came through
from those consultations that we prepared a report and then we've prepared a campaign
which was launched recently and - you are probably coming to this in terms of the
campaign, so I will stop there now.

MS HEGER SC: I will come to the campaign. In terms of the findings of the report, in
the Executive Summary on page 10, it's noted that community members told the
Commission it was vital to understand that the experience of affected communities was not
the same and the harms or racism vary across different people and different groups. But at
the same time the report noted that some common themes emerged. Could I ask you
describe what those common themes were?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes. So in terms of the common themes, what
consistently came through - and sometimes - I went to a lot of these consultations, and
I remember thinking, "I could have heard this in any one of the consultations", the same
thing that was said to me and it was - and I know you are going to get more evidence about
this later today, but that sense of being dehumanised; that sense of being seen as lesser, as
not an equal participant in society; that sense of being subject - you or your community
subject to mis- and disinformation particularly online, being subject to tropes and
stereotypes; that sense of having to hide aspects of your identity in public or in workplaces.
That was a very common theme across all communities.
A sense of being pitted against each, that is, that communities - we would hear regularly,
"Why are you just consulting with us? Why aren't you bringing everyone in together so
you can hear from everyone?" And we'd often have to say, "well, we are trying to hear
from everyone but we're doing it bit by bit or we're doing it within the limitations of this
project". Another theme that came up consistently was "you need to talk to Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander peoples if you want to understand how racism operates in this
country”, which wasn't within the scope of the project. Another thing that came up was
negative - consistently across all communities, negative portrayal within the media:
stereotypes, failing to properly inform yourselves before broadcasting a story, or whatever
it might be.
Another thing that came up was consistently viewing communities from a deficit lens
rather than the strengths that communities bring through their diversity and their history,
and connected to that, was - what consistently came up was a lack of understanding of how
these communities are an integral part of the fabric of Australian society and have been
for - well, since colonialisation, effectively, or even before so in terms of the Muslim
community and Makassan traders. So those were, I think, the major common themes
across all of the communities.
MS HEGER SC: What were the Commission's findings in terms of what, if any,
difference there was in those communities' experience of racism after October 7, as
opposed to before?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: For all communities, it had increased significantly.
And how it particularly manifested for each community, of course, is different, and - but
they all highlighted that it had increased online stratospherically for many communities.
Some people were telling us that they just were not online anymore because it was such an
unsafe place to be. It had increased in workplaces, and workplaces ended up being a really
consistent theme that came up as an area where people felt disadvantaged, isolated, they
felt they couldn't express their identity, felt that they were in danger of losing their job, felt

that there wasn't a safe space to have difficult conversations. So all of those were things
that had increased after October 7.
MS HEGER SC: I see. And in your statement, you noted it was not an objective of this
project to identify areas for action, but, nevertheless, during the consultations, community
members did identify some priority areas for action and you give some examples of those
at paragraph 37 of your statement. To what extent did those priority areas marry up with
the recommendations made in the Anti-Racism Framework? Maybe you could give some
examples of the parallels?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes, I mean, they completely married up with the
recommendations in the National Anti-Racism Framework, which wasn't surprising to us
at all because the framework came out of significant consultation with the same
communities, including individual and group consultation. So what came through in terms
of what should be done, what communities asked for, was better understanding of racism
and the capacity to address it within workplaces, education and legal systems, and
that - and within government, and that's directly relevant to our recommendations on
workplaces and the justice system. Improving the Racial Discrimination Act or addressing
gaps within it, that is directly relevant to our duty about including a positive duty in the
Racial Discrimination Act.
Reviewing the impact of laws and how they might disproportionately affect some
communities, that's something we recommend in our framework. Mandating anti-racism
training for politicians; that was a theme that came through very consistently, and that is
that there is a very specific recommendation in our framework about parliamentarians
conducting anti-racism training. Because if our leaders don't exhibit the behaviours that
the rest of us should do then what hope do we have?
Improving the way media reports on communities, as I mentioned earlier, then we have
a specific part of our framework that focuses on the media and building racial literacy
within the media. And we did, during the course of the development of the framework,
release a media - a Race Reporting Handbook in conjunction with Media Diversity
Australia. Reform of digital platforms, again as I said earlier, the online environment was
a theme that came up all the time in terms of how hostile and unsafe it is for all
communities.
Helping people have difficult conversations about Gaza and working with local
communities to do that, and that relates to our recommendation about working with
communities to come up - and designing with communities solutions that impact on those
communities. And then trauma-informed training for workplaces. Again, that's something
that we point to in recommendation 20. Then the overarching idea, which I've talked about
previously, that is don't pit communities against each other. Come up with solutions that
help everyone, which is the starting point of the National Anti-Racism Framework.
MS HEGER SC: You mentioned the campaign that was aligned to this earlier. It that the
Change the System, Change the Story campaign?

COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Correct.
MS HEGER SC: I might ask you about that now. The Commission launched that
campaign in July of this year?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Correct.
MS HEGER SC: And what was that prompted by? Was it prompted by the consultation
undertaken as part of the Seen & Heard project?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes. So it was - in the consultations, workplace
continuously came through as a significant area where people were impacted. The
campaign videos actually used direct quotes from the consultations that people had
experienced, racist things that were said, but in a systemic way. Things that weren't direct
slurs but were a way in which policies and processes diminish people. And we also
thought that workplaces was an area where we could, in a campaign like this, have
a significant impact.
MS HEGER SC: And so what is the key message of the campaign in terms of
workplaces?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: The key message is that racism often hides in plain
sight. It hides within policies and processes that might appear neutral on their face, but
they are not because they disadvantage some communities. They force them to shed
themselves of their culture, their religion, their identity, the things that make them different
so that they can fit into the workplace and progress. So it's a campaign that's targeted at
managers and leaders of workplaces, executives, to really have a hard look at the way in
which the organisation might disadvantage and diminish different people of different racial
backgrounds.
MS HEGER SC: And it was part of the campaign, was it, to develop what you describe
as campaign assets? What were those assets?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: The primary - yes, it was. The primary asset are
a series of campaign videos, and there is what's called a "hero video", which has a number
of different communities represented where you see the quotes, as I said, directly from our
consultations where people were being erased, and you see that - the visual is a person
disintegrates and then they're brought back together when you have the more positive
quotes about what you can do.
MS HEGER SC: How are those videos deployed and who were the target audience?
Was the idea that they be shown in workplaces or on social media or what was the intent
behind the videos?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: So it's a combination. So we deployed them on
YouTube and LinkedIn, primarily because you can turn the comments off, and this
is - I should mention it. It's a terrible thing. We had some specific videos where one was

very specifically for the Jewish community with just Jewish people represented. One was
specifically the Palestinian and Muslim community. When we initially put those up, the
torrent of racism towards the respective communities and abuse to the Commission for
having done this was terrible. And it just kind of highlighted the point. And a lot of that
was about, "Why are you just focusing on these people? They don't deserve it", et cetera,
et cetera.
And I think that was case in point as to why you need to be broader in the way in which
you approach racism, but it can also be tailored. So the hero video is broad, many different
people represented, but tailored because you can definitely identify specific communities
within that hero video. And in addition to the videos, we have posters and then we have
a set of resources on our website or on the landing page for that campaign that assists
employers. And the deployment wasn't just YouTube and LinkedIn. It was also, we sent it
to a whole variety of employer representatives who just wanted to get their hands on it,
because they said "this is going to be really great for us to use and to distribute amongst
workplaces". And I do have some statistics, if you want to know how well it has been
viewed.
MS HEGER SC: Are those the ones you set out at paragraph 60?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Well, I've got updated statistics that are even better,
so that's why I thought -
MS HEGER SC: Yes, please let us know.
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: So as of today, we have got 2.5 million impressions
of the video and 1.6 million completed video views, which is actually very - it's excellent.
So that means 1.6 million people have sat through the whole thing.
MS HEGER SC: At paragraph 58, you note that the campaign asks people who lead
Australian workplaces to take responsibility for making them free of racism, and it asks
them to do three things: Listen to the experiences of the people around them, learn where
racism is showing up in their own system, and lead the changes that fix it. Does that - that
seems to have a parallel with what you were saying earlier about how you might go about
fulfilling a positive duty to eliminate racism in the workplace. Is that right?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Exactly, yes. That is, you can't assume that you
know what the problem is or you know the extent of the problem - and most organisations
will assume there's no problem - whereas if you are prepared to listen to your workforce,
you can actually get a sense of what that issue is. And then the second part, the "learn"
part, yes, as I said that is parallel to all. It marries up with what I said about consultation
and understanding what your workforce is experiencing. The "learn" is parallel to ask your
workforce what solutions will be effective, particularly for particular communities. And
then the "lead" part is about bringing about the change, that is, having the courage to show
that you are going to change the systems to make them better.

MS HEGER SC: And you have noted that the Human Rights Commission has limited
ongoing resources to continue this campaign and no capacity to upscale it. If resources
were available, is this campaign something that you consider would be useful to continue?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes, I think there are great opportunities to expand
the campaign, to go out and talk to specific workforces and large employers about it. Also,
to monitor and evaluate how effective we think it is. But we can't do any of that because
the funding comes to an absolute halt very shortly.
MS HEGER SC: I see. Could I then ask you a bit more about the role of the Human
Rights Commission regarding complaints, and you have addressed this from paragraph 65
of your statement. Could you just describe for us in general terms what its role is in
relation to the investigation and conciliation of complaints?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: So the role of the Commission - and this is - it's
vested in the President - is to impartially inquire into and attempt to conciliate complaints
of unlawful discrimination under the various Acts that give you that power. Relevant
probably to this Commission is the Racial Discrimination Act.
MS HEGER SC: And does that role extend to investigation and conciliation of
complaints under section 18C of the Racial Discrimination Act?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: It does.
MS HEGER SC: Which, of course, prohibits acts that are reasonably likely to offend
where the act is done because of race, colour or national or ethnic origin of a person?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Correct, it does.
MS HEGER SC: And the Commission has already received some evidence about the
work done, for example, by some members of the Jewish community to bring proceedings
under that provision and I think the Human Rights Commission's own submission refers to,
for example, the case against Wissam Haddad. What would you say to the suggestion that
the Human Rights Commission should be given the power to bring applications itself
under section 18C of the Racial Discrimination Act, possibly to alleviate the burden on
community members to bring those sorts of claims?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Obviously we want access to justice for those
people targeted by racial discrimination, and there have been some recent changes to the
legal framework that would help this, including creating an asymmetrical cost obligation
so that applicants are less likely to bear the burden of costs and also allowing for
representative complaints. This particular idea, I'm not sure if it is one that would assist,
because the important thing, as I said earlier, our conciliations process - investigation and
conciliations process is impartial, and, most importantly, has to be seen as impartial, has to
be seen as a place where people can go to access justice without fear of any bias.

If a Commissioner like me was able to bring a complaint, I think that would undermine
that perception of bias because a person - a respondent, for example, to a complaint of
racial vilification or discrimination, could feel concern that if the complaint didn't resolve,
I could then seek to bring a proceeding on the same ground or even effectively take over
that proceeding, and that would mean that I had a view on it, and that - the perception
could obviously be that that would influence the conciliation process. So I think that it's
damaging - or potentially damaging the perception of impartiality for what is very, very
important function in our society that is done very well by our investigation and
complaints team is not worth the risk.
MS HEGER SC: I see. And when complaints of that kind are brought under section 18C
of the Racial Discrimination Act or other kinds of complaints, there's also provision in the
Act for the Human Rights Commission to act as an amicus.
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Correct.
MS HEGER SC: So how would that role be impacted if a suggestion like this were
implemented?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes, it's hard to see how you could reconcile the two
different roles. I mean, the amicus role is very clearly one to assist the court. It's not about
acting on behalf of either party. It's about assisting the court, particularly where there's a
question of law, as I did recently in the case of the Faruqi v Hanson. So I think that that
amicus curiae function is probably a better mechanism because it maintains the
impartiality and makes clear that the Commissioner is impartial to either party, but allows
the Commission to at least assist the court in determining a particular point about racial
discrimination.
MS HEGER SC: You mentioned earlier two recent reforms intended to reduce barriers to
complainants, one being the cost reforms and there's also the facility to bring
representative proceedings. In relation to that second category, representative proceedings,
you have identified in your statement a proposed reform that you consider could make the
bringing of those proceedings easier. Could you explain what that reform involves?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: So it could be further simplified by removing the
requirement for the representative body that currently exists to have the written consent of
all representatives represented. That is quite an onerous administrative burden. And we
say that that, removing that particular requirement, would make it easier to bring
representative complaints and enable access to justice.
MS HEGER SC: I see. What sort of consultations have you undertaken in relation to that
proposed reform to date?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: I haven't, myself, because I'm separate to the
complaints process. So probably I can't speak to consultation, myself.

MS HEGER SC: I see. Thank you. Commissioner, I have no further questions of
Commissioner Sivaraman.
COMMISSIONER: I've only got one more. You mentioned a publication that had been
distributed to the media relating to how they might best report on issues touching on
racism. What was that publication?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: It's called the Race Reporting Handbook, and it was
done in conjunction with the Australian Human Rights Commission and Media Diversity
Australia.
COMMISSIONER: Was that distributed to all of the mainstream media outlets in
Australia?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Correct, it was, because they are - most of them are
members of Media Diversity Australia. Whether they act on it or not is another question,
but it has certainly been distributed to them.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, thank you.
MS HEGER SC: I understand Mr Bender had some questions.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, indeed. Yes, Mr Bender.
MR BENDER SC: Commissioner Sivaraman, my name is Bender. I appear for seven
peak Jewish community bodies. The Human Rights Commission has filed a submission
dated 12 June 2026 to this Royal Commission, and you're one of the signatories to the
foreword of that submission made by the Human Rights Commission. In the foreword
there's an acknowledgement that - and if you have it, for your convenience, page 5 - there
are many unique aspects to antisemitism and some of the examples that are given are the
diversity within the Jewish population in Australia. Another example is the tendency to
hold Australian Jews collectively responsible for the actions of the State of Israel.
I'm going to ask you about several other what I'm going to suggest are distinctive features
of antisemitism, to get your views about whether you agree, and I want you to be clear, I'm
not asking you to agree that antisemitism is any less important or more important than any
other form of discrimination, nor that other forms of discrimination aren't also distinctive
and unique in their own ways. Do you understand?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes.
MR BENDER SC: So, firstly, antisemitism often attributes power to Jews rather than
inferiority. For example, Jews are often portrayed by antisemites as controlling the media
or the government. Do you agree with that?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Can I just preface my answer in this way: That is,
when I respond to your questions, I do so on the basis of my consultations with the Jewish

community because they - the way in which racism has targeted them has informed me. I
have been very lucky to have a lot of consultation with the Jewish community, very
privileged to do so. So I will just put it in that context. It's not just me pontificating from
up on high; it's actually from my consultations. And with that, yes, the answer is that that
trope or stereotype is certainly one that I've been told is antisemitic in nature. Whether or
not it doesn't - it's never been used for any other community, I can't speak to, but certainly
it's one that is prevalent in antisemitic online and elsewhere material.
MR BENDER SC: So training of racism generally or in respect of racism generally that
focuses on portrayals of inferiority might not necessarily pick up that aspect of
antisemitism; would you agree with that?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: If there's training - I wouldn't even recommend
training focusing on inferiority. That's the thing. Because we believe that the way in
which you approach anti-racism training is to talk about the strength that communities
bring, their contribution to our history, to our culture and so on. So I actually think it's
a dangerous thing to - I wouldn't recommend focusing on inferiority at all because I think
then you are often playing into tropes. I understand - I think where you're going with this
is probably to say that trope isn't relevant to the Jewish community, but in a sense it's
a damaging thing to do at all.
I think it's more about building racial literacy. So to understand why someone is
determined - just - I use myself as an example. Like, I go to - I fly to Chenai, the city I
was born in India and I'm Giri or Giridharan. And I get on the plane and I come home to
Australia and suddenly I become ethnic or multicultural or I'm diverse. I'm exactly the
same person that boarded that plane and came home, but I've been made different by the
society around me. Understanding how you have been made different, often by respect to
what is the norm, is critical to building racial literacy. And, of course, when it comes to
the Jewish community, you would consult with the community to understand how is it that
you've been differentiated to the norm. And that, I think, is the more effective way to
proceed.
MR BENDER SC: Secondly, other than the trope of attributing power to Jews, you
would agree there are several other antisemitic tropes that are particular to antisemitism;
it's not the only one?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes.
MR BENDER SC: And in order to detect them and address them requires an
understanding and literacy in the language of that antisemitic trope history; do you agree?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes. And I should just say, sorry, just because it's
relevant to your question, you talk about the history. The point is that the manifestations
of racism, including antisemitism, will change over time. So, yes, you would look at the
history, but you would also have to look at it - you would have to talk to people now,
Jewish people now, about what is your experience of antisemitism, how have you been

targeted by antisemitism, because you can't assume that the way in which it has targeted
people 30 years ago is necessarily the way in which it is targeting people now.
MR BENDER SC: Indeed. You are ahead of me, Commissioner Sivaraman, because the
third feature I was about to ask you about was that evolving nature of antisemitism, which
is an old, old hatred that has changed over eons and continues to change, and it's a
particularly distinctive nature of antisemitism that isn't present in all other forms of racism;
do you agree?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: It's difficult to answer that question because, yes of
course I say that the nature of antisemitism has changed over time and, of course, it is an
old form of racism. But it's the last point, "it's not applicable to all other forms of racism".
That's such a generalised statement. I just don't think I could agree to that in good
conscience because how can I speak for all other forms of racism? I just can't.
MR BENDER SC: Fourthly, Holocaust denial and distortion have some analogues in
other forms of racism; certainly other groups of people who have had atrocities committed
to them and then those atrocities have been denied. But can I suggest Holocaust denial has
a real distinctiveness in respect of antisemitism, first because of the scale of the Holocaust,
but also because it tends to depict Jews as having a fraudulent claim to victimhood. Do
you agree with that?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Sorry, could you just repeat that question again?
There were a few parts to it.
MR BENDER SC: Sorry, it was a long question.
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes.
MR BENDER SC: So, first of all, I'm not suggesting that Jewish people are the only
people who have suffered atrocities that have been denied; do you understand?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes.
MR BENDER SC: But I am suggesting that Holocaust denial is a distinctive aspect of
antisemitism compared to other forms of racism, first, because of the scale of the
Holocaust and its relative recency; do you agree?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes, I think it has to be a distinctive aspect of
antisemitism because it is such a distinct event. So, in that sense, yes.
MR BENDER SC: Fifthly, the evidence heard by the Royal Commission includes
evidence of increasing antisemitism manifesting in progressive spaces. So in, for example,
the submission from the Human Rights Commission, there's evidence of
a survey - paragraph 183 - that 93.8 per cent of religious and 81 per cent of secular Jewish
respondents reported experiencing direct or indirect racism at a university. Do you recall
that part of the Commission submission?

COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Yes, I recall that part of the university study, yes.
MR BENDER SC: So I suggest that a distinctive aspect of antisemitism is that it's
growing in spaces that are progressive and one would expect to be tolerant; do you agree?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Again, I think that's such a difficult question to
answer because over what time period and relevant to - by respect to what - I'm not trying
to be difficult. I think my point is this: You've talked about the increase in antisemitism.
It's increased; we know that. That's come through from communities. How much and
where and how, that is a problem with our lack of consistent national data collection on
antisemitism and other forms of racism. Without being able to do that, you don't even
have a baseline up against which you can measure what is increasing and how it is
increasing. So I don't want to, say, give you a simple answer to that question because it
undermines what I think is a fundamental systemic problem with the way in which we
monitor racism in this country that needs to be fixed.
MR BENDER SC: So you don't agree that antisemitism is increasing in progressive
spaces, including universities?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: No, antisemitism is clearly prevalent in universities,
and that's what our study showed. But our studies are baseline. There was no such study
done previously. It's the first time it has ever been done. So it showed it to be at
alarmingly high rates, without question, and that would, of course, mean it's - if
a university represents a broad political spectrum all up, then it's going to be on all aspects
of that. Whether it has increased in a particular aspect, university, like, well, how do you
know without - that's the whole point. You don't have a baseline against which to measure
it.
MR BENDER SC: I suggest that the increase in progressive spaces, including
universities, of antisemitism, while not unique to antisemitism, is a distinctive feature of it.
Do you agree with that?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: I guess - it's - I'm not sure if I can answer that, for
the reasons I've just given in terms of not having a baseline for measurement.
MR BENDER SC: I understand. Next, do you agree that no other Australian community
schools and places of worship operate behind armed guards and bulletproof glass?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: Other than Jewish ones, you mean?
MR BENDER SC: Yes.
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: No, I've been told there are some Muslim religious
institutions or places of worship that do have armed security. So this is just in my
engagement with those communities. So very sadly - it's a terrible thing that Jewish
schools and places of worship have to have armed guards. That is a terrible, terrible thing.

I don't - from my engagement, it doesn't, unfortunately, sadly, doesn't seem to be only
those institutions now.
MR BENDER SC: Very sadly, both Jewish and Muslim schools now have to have those
protections, and I suggest that is a distinctive feature of antisemitism or a consequence of
antisemitism, but it may not necessarily be a unique consequence to Jewish people; do you
agree?
COMMISSIONER SIVARAMAN: It's - when you - it's not a distinct feature of
antisemitism in the sense of it's the way in which it's responded to. What I think it reflects
is that there is a distinct threat of violence associated with antisemitism. That is
not - unfortunately, that is not isolated to the Jewish community. We have seen and I've
had consultations that have showed acts of violence and destruction to other places of
worship. And if you just cast your mind back a few decades, it wasn't that long ago that,
for example, we had firebombing of Chinese restaurants in Western Australia. So this
notion of racist violence - or we saw the attempted attack at an Invasion Day rally in
Boorloo, Perth. Unfortunately, racist violence toward any particular cohort is a very real
and - threat. How those communities respond varies. But it is not isolated to one

Centre, you have participated in two long walks that you describe in your statement.
Could you address those, please, for the Commissioner?
THE HON PETER GUTWEIN: Absolutely. In 2024, as we have seen around this
country, unfortunately, there have been rising incidences of racism occurring now over
a handful of years. And one weekend, one Sunday morning, I was reading our local
newspaper and it was outlining the fact that two taxi drivers had been racially vilified on
Friday in Hobart and had been beaten, largely because of their colour. And my initial
thought was to - as I had done in the past, was to put out a press statement and call it out,
and which we did, but I must admit, I was thinking that morning that if I do this, you
know, once again within a couple of days that statement is forgotten. It's just an
ex-Premier, head of the Migrant Resource Centre calling out this particular issue. You
know, people move on.
So I thought what could I do that could change the narrative here in Tasmania? What can
I do that might have some form of enduring impact. So the concept of walking across
Tasmania and along the way being joined by migrants and refugees and providing them
with the opportunity, a platform, if you like, to share their contribution, both economically
and socially, to Tasmania and to build into the public discourse here the understanding of
what people are bringing when they do arrive here in Tasmania; things like, for example,
here in Launceston, if you have a sick child, their life will more than likely be saved by an

Indian or a Sri Lankan paediatrician. On the north-west coast, I walked for a period of
time with an Indian doctor who had been in that community for over a quarter of century,
had supported families, improved health and given birth and had made a singular, very
strong contribution to that community.
In the Central Midlands, I met with fruit pickers and berry pickers that were here on
PALM visas, helping to ensure that our farms and agriculture continue. And so we told
their stories. I also bumped in an Egyptian in Campbelltown, who runs for - in the centre
of Tasmania, the only cancer infusion centre that operates out of a major capital city so that
anybody across the state that wants chemotherapy or other services can actually travel to
the centre of Tasmania and not need to travel further to get those services. And so through
that first walk it was a matter of trying to reset the narrative here and have people focus on
the positive and to try to have them gain some understanding of the contribution that
migrants and refugees were making here in Tasmania.
One fabulous contribution was by a young Indian fellow who had arrived in this country in
Sydney in 2018-19 to study a Master's of Accountancy and he had been derailed in that
pursuit through COVID, decided that he needed to ensure that he could sustain himself, so
he pivoted into a building apprenticeship. In the same month that he qualified for his
Master's of Accountancy, he also qualified as a qualified builder and now lives in
Tasmania, building houses for Tasmanians whilst building a life for himself. They were
the sorts of stories that we told on that walk.
MR LANCASTER SC: Thank you. And you've also recounted a second walk from
Launceston to Canberra as the start and end points, but you have identified a particular
impetus for that walk occurring. Could you address that?
THE HON PETER GUTWEIN: I could, and the Commission should understand once I
finished that first walk which was seven days and 350 kilometres, I vowed never to do
a long distance walk again. But within the next couple of months the Multicultural
Framework Review had been handed down which was a significant piece of work and
perhaps one of the more stringent reviews of the multicultural sector that's been completed
in this country. And it was handed down. There were 29 different recommendations that
were included in it.
The first recommendation and the recommendations were prioritised. I thought it was very
apt that this recommendation sat at number 1 and that was that the federal parliament
should come together and it should reaffirm its commitment to multicultural Australia.
Now, I think most people understand that with 30 per cent of our population born overseas
and around 50 per cent of people having at least one parent that was born overseas, we are
a multicultural country. That is what we are. But with the change in the tide in terms of
the national discourse and in terms of the rising incidences of racial vilification that we
were seeing here, I thought that it was an ideal opportunity for the federal government at
that time to take that opportunity and to make that reaffirmation in the national parliament.
Now, it hadn't happened. It didn't happen. And so I decided to walk to Canberra to speak
with the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition, and set out from Launceston to

do so. I received a lot of support along the way from corporations and individuals and
from migrant communities. And I arrived in Canberra after seven days; met with the
Prime Minister, met with the Leader of the Opposition. The Prime Minister made an
affirmation along those lines in parliament. The Leader of the Opposition then spoke
positively about what I was attempting to do. But I think the missed opportunity was that
parliament didn't take the opportunity for a debate, and to admit, through a vote to that
concept of reaffirming Australia as a multicultural country.
MR LANCASTER SC: From your perspective, as a former state premier, what makes
such affirmations by governments and leaders significant in this context?
THE HON PETER GUTWEIN: I think the - what everybody is looking for is leadership
on issues like this. And, you know, one of the reasons why - I was speaking to one of the
authors only recently in terms of that Multicultural Framework Review - why this
reaffirmation of Australia as a multicultural country was listed as number 1 was because,
broadly speaking, those that had put that report together felt that it was a very important
recommendation.
You know, what politicians, what members of parliament say does matter. You know, the
words that they use are the tools of their trade, and they can build cathedrals or they can
tear them down. And in this case 50 years on from when Al Grassby first spoke about
Australia as a multicultural country, it was a great opportunity, I think, to send a signal to
all of this country that we have - our roots are in migration, immigration, save for First
Nations, all of us arrived here from somewhere else.
MR LANCASTER SC: Against that background in 2025 you became a member of the
Australian Multicultural Council and in July this year, 2026, you were appointed as Chair
of that body; correct?
THE HON PETER GUTWEIN: That's correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: And can you explain what the Australian Multicultural Council
is and its primary functions?
THE HON PETER GUTWEIN: Well, the Council consists now of around 13 members;
all of them from different states and territories. There are eight that are jointly nominated
by the federal government along with state governments; and then there are five members
that are ministerial appointed, of which I was one. That council's role in terms of
multiculturalism, inclusion, is to provide advice to the federal government in regards to
matters relating to our multicultural society, the types of policy that might be introduced,
to provide feedback as well to relevant ministers.
We served two, Minister Aly as our chief minister, and to Assistant Minister Julian Hill
who recently met with the Council when we had my first meeting a couple of weeks ago
again.

MR LANCASTER SC: Thank you. You referred a little earlier in your evidence to your
preference over the description "social cohesion" of a description of "living well together".
And one of the key messages you bring forward in your statement is the importance of the
way leaders in particular talk about social cohesion or living well together, and that it
should not be left to the migrant communities to do their own work in that regard. Could
you elaborate on that reflection?
THE HON PETER GUTWEIN: In terms of living well together and the role that
migrant communities play and migrant organisations play, obviously they have a voice and
they should use it. But I think that there are a range of other organisations as well that
should be at the table and should be supportive and, importantly, should be sharing the
contribution that migrants and refugees make to this country.
Consider organisations like the Business Council and chambers of commerce, housing
industry associations, all who benefit from the skills that migrants bring, and also
understand very clearly the challenges that this country has, you know, with the low
unemployment rates, (indistinct) with skills challenges, I think it's important that those
sorts of voices are heard in the debate and that they take strong and positive positions.
You know, too often a migrant voice or somebody representing a migrant organisation will
be dismissed as simply arguing for themselves. Whereas I think this is a broader issue and
there needs to be a broader conversation and the more voices that can be brought to hear
that debate, the better.
MR LANCASTER SC: You've also noted the capacity for personal stories and anecdotes
to be an effective tool for building broader community and social understanding about
other members of the community. And you've shared one of those anecdotes in your
statement relating to your time as premier during the COVID pandemic. Would you care
to share that with the Commissioner?
THE HON PETER GUTWEIN: Look, I would. Early on in COVID when we were
facing, or moving towards the first lockdown and it was understood very clearly across the
country, at a leadership level, that those most at risk would be those that were older or
those that had some form of health issue. And as we headed into the first lockdown I had
messaged very strongly, as did other premiers, that, you know, stay home, stay safe, only
leave for certain reasons.
And, as I say, it leans into the fact that - and knowing full well that Tasmania had one of
the older populations out of all the states and territories, it lent very heavily into that. As
we moved into the first week, I'd said to my staff that we will get - and we understood that
we would be getting thousands of pieces of either correspondence or contact with officers
in government, and there would be a lot reaching out to the premier's office directly. And
I'd indicated to them that each night, what I would do finish the day off would be to make
phone calls to the people that they felt that I should talk to, either to provide them
understanding of why we were doing what we were doing, or some - provide some level of
confidence or just be near to listen to, which I was on many occasions.

And on the second day, my executive assistant provided me with a list, and there was
a message from a lady that she described as a 90 year old war widow, and she said, "I don't
know if I should give you this one." I said, "Why is that?" She said, "She wants to speak
about the Asians next door." And I said, "Look, well, I'm up for that. I will have that
conversation", because we had seen some rising incidences of racism, pushback against
foreign students earlier in the year as COVID became an understood reality. And so
I picked up the phone and I spoke to this lady. And she explained to me that she
lived - she had lived next door to, as she put it, this Asian family for the last 10 years.
They shared paths to the mailbox and out to the street, and in 10 years, she had never - and
nor had they spoken to her, and she had never made an approach.
And she said, "I just want to let you know that on that first night after you messaged that
we needed to stay home to stay safe, that there was a knock at the door". And she said,
"I opened it and I was surprised that it was the Asian family, or the mum and the dad."
And she said - they said, "Look, we heard the premier's message, about staying safe. We
were wondering if you would like us to go and do your shopping for you." And she said,
"Look, I raised this with you," she said, "just so that you understand that the type of
Tasmania that you are leading has this type of goodness, this type of people in it."
I had to admit I shed a tear in that phone call, and three months later she reached out again
and left a message that the family that she was living next to, who were from Sri Lanka by
the way, that her children were now treating her as a de facto grandmother. I think what
was really interesting from that was that there was an understanding: here were two - here
were good people that just never had the opportunity to connect but when they did they
formed a bond and they found that it was breaking common ground.
MR LANCASTER SC: Thank you. In your statement you make the observation that in
your view successive federal and state governments, despite best endeavours, have at times
lost control of the debate about the need for coordinating resources to reshape the narrative
in respect of social cohesion or living well together; and you make the observation that
divisive voices should not be allowed to craft the messaging, in your words. Could you
explain your view of how leadership bears on the national narrative?
THE HON PETER GUTWEIN: Well, I think leadership and communication is so very
important, and I'll come back to that point that I made about - I think that the priority
recommendation 1 out of the Framework Review, to have the parliament come together
and make a reaffirmation that Australia as a multicultural country, I think is so very
important. I think that in itself could help reshape the narrative.
But there is no doubt at the moment that those that would seek to use immigration,
migration more broadly, as a weapon and look to have a grievance debate and point to
a range of matters and blame immigration for it, you know, are doing that. And I think
those that are opposed to migration or want to use migration, as I say, as a political
weapon, are honing their narrative and have created it already.
You know, "Migration has pushed up the cost of housing. Migrants have taken my job."
They have a simple but brutal message, and I think there is a real need in this country for

a national narrative to be developed, one that can point to the value and the contribution
that people from so many different countries, so many different backgrounds, have made in
a positive sense to Australia.
I will give you an example of what I mean. Early on, and this occurred prior to taking on
the first walk and I had reached out to a gentleman who ran one of the major infrastructure
and civil companies in Tasmania. I was looking for somebody to either make a donation
or provide some support to assist me as I walked on the national highways. They're not the
safest place to walk in any state. And I asked if he would assist me and he asked me what
I was doing and I said I was wanting to share the contribution migrants and refugees were
making in a positive sense and his answer was, "Whatever you need you can have. Just
tell me and I'll do it." I asked him, I said, "Why are you doing that?" And he said, "Look,
back in the 1970s when we had the French and the Germans, the Italians, the Yugoslavs,
the Greeks, you know, and a range of other nationalities arrived here" - and I hope I can
use the language that he used - and he said, "I treated them like wogs." He said, "Many
people did." He said, "Today", he said, "those people are members of my family. They're
members of my business."
He said, "We can't wait 30 to 40 years now for Australians to accept the current migrants
that we have in the same way that it took us 30 to 40 years to accept that last wave." And
it's interesting: when you look at the contribution that was made through the 60s and 70s
in terms of some of the major infrastructure works that have gone on in this country, the
Snowy River Scheme, the Hydro in Tasmania, most Australians and certainly most
Tasmanians if you mention the Hydro look at that period and the people that came and
built that infrastructure, they look back with a sense of pride and gratitude.
We have got to start the narrative now in terms of the migrants that we have in this
country; the fact that we have doctors, the fact that we have engineers, you know, people
are working on our farms. They're the stories that have got to be told because unlike 30
years ago, today we have the internet. And social media is no longer a platform; it's
become a battleground. It took us 30 years to find a way to look back with pride on the
contribution the migrants of the 60s and 70s made. It will take us even longer if we allow
the narrative to get away from us now that, unfortunately, social media is playing a role as
well.
MR LANCASTER SC: And in that process of building a narrative, you've indicated in
your statement the significance of the role of leaders in the corporate sector and civil
society and the political spectrum as well; is that right?
THE HON PETER GUTWEIN: I think that everybody needs to lean into this. Now, if
you think about the wall of work that is in front of this country over the next decade: you
know, South-East Queensland in the preparation for the Olympics, here in Tasmania the
building of a billion dollar stadium, some of the infrastructure projects and commitments
that were made by governments and were still undelivered that were made during the
COVID period. You know, there is a significant amount of work this country has in front
of it, and we need migration to ensure that we have got the skills to deal with that task.

And I think that the voices of the chambers of commerce and the business associations, the
housing industry associations, they all need to be, you know, heard and be a part of the
national narrative. Importantly, you know, I think there is a need for us to think deeply
and carefully about the role that government plays in terms of supporting the creation and
the delivery of a national narrative. For example - I was only looking last week at this - we
spent, I think it was three-quarters of a billion dollars on the census, on counting our
population and understanding our population, of which there was around $40 million set
aside for ensuring that people understood what they needed to do. You know, I would like
to see - I think the fact that we have a multicultural society means that we should be
investing in ensuring that that multicultural society can be successful.
Governments of all persuasions, state and federal, will invest in the assets that they need
to, to maintain them: our roads, our schools, our hospitals; they will invest in
infrastructure for energy, water and sewage. I would posit that our single most important
asset we have in this country is our people, and I think that there is a role for government
to play in creating a national narrative that talks to both the struggle and the challenge that
we see migrants and refugees happening, importantly also the great contribution that they
make to this country, and I think there's an educative piece there and a role for government
to play in that.
MR LANCASTER SC: Mr Gutwein, thank you very much for your evidence. I don't
have any further questions.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, thank you, Mr Gutwein. You are now excused.
THE HON PETER GUTWEIN: Thank you very much.
